title: Bumped from a flight? What US airlines owe you
summary: Involuntarily bumped from an overbooked US flight? Here's the DOT cash minimum you're owed, when airlines can skip it, and how to claim.
body_markdown:
Jake was at the gate for a Denver–Chicago flight when the agent got on the mic: the flight was oversold, and they needed volunteers before they started picking names. Nobody took the offer, so the airline picked for them — and Jake was one of them. He figured that was just how it goes with overbooked flights: annoying, but nothing he could do about it. He was wrong. Most people assume US airlines can wriggle out of paying for this the same way they do for delays and cancellations. They can't — bumping is one of the few disruptions where federal law hands you a guaranteed cash number, on the spot, no negotiation required.


## What you're owed, at a glance


Flight distance


Compensation


Within 1 hour of your original arrival time


None required


1–2 hours late domestic (1–4 hours international)


200% of your one-way fare, up to $1,075


More than 2 hours late domestic (more than 4 hours international), or no substitute flight offered


400% of your one-way fare, up to $2,150


Paid in cash or by check, on the spot — not a travel voucher. Airlines can offer a voucher instead, but you don't have to take it.


## When this applies — and when it doesn't


This covers you on any US domestic flight, and on international flights departing a US airport on any airline, when you're involuntarily bumped because of overbooking, a smaller aircraft swap, or a weight-and-balance restriction.


It doesn't apply if:


-


You volunteered to give up your seat — there's no legal minimum for that; whatever you negotiate at the gate is the deal.


-


You didn't check in or reach the gate by the airline's deadline.


-


You're on an aircraft with 30 or fewer seats, which falls outside the DOT oversales rule.


-


You're on a codeshare operated by a foreign carrier not otherwise subject to DOT rules.


The one thing worth being clear-eyed about: US law doesn't require airlines to pay cash for a delayed or canceled flight — that's where the "US doesn't really compensate you" reputation comes from. Bumping is the exception. It's the one scenario where 14 CFR Part 250 gives you a fixed, mandatory cash payout, separate from any refund or rebooking.


### Jake's edge case: no substitute flight offered


Here's where Jake's story gets more interesting. The airline couldn't offer him anything until the next morning — no substitute flight at all that day. Because no alternate transportation was arranged, he jumped straight to the 400% tier, even though a same-day reroute landing him two hours late might otherwise have only triggered the 200% rate. (If your ticket doesn't show a fare — an award ticket, say — compensation is based on the lowest cash fare charged for a seat in the same class on that flight, not a token amount.) Jake asked the gate agent to confirm the calculation in writing, and walked away with a check before he left the airport.


## What to do if you're bumped


1.


**Don't volunteer** until you've heard the number. There's no legal floor for voluntary bumping, so it's worth negotiating before you put your hand up.


2.


**Name the rule** . Tell the agent: "I understand my involuntary denied boarding compensation is 200% or 400% of my fare, in cash or by check." Naming it tends to speed things along.


3.


**Ask for cash or a check** , not just a voucher — you're entitled to it, and a voucher is only an alternative you can choose, not the default.


4.


**Keep your original ticket.** You can still use it on another flight, or request a refund for the unused portion if you'd rather not travel.


5.


**Get the calculation in writing** before you leave the airport.


## Flying to or from Europe? You might be covered twice over


Jake's story doesn't end at Denver. A few months later, he was flying Chicago to Rome and back on a US airline — and it turns out his trip had two different rulebooks attached to it, not one.


Here's the rule EU261 actually uses, and it has nothing to do with your passport: it looks at where the flight departs from and which airline operates it.


-


**Departing the EU or UK:** covered under EC 261/UK 261 on any airline — American, Delta, United, doesn't matter — regardless of your nationality.


-


**Arriving in the EU or UK from elsewhere:** only covered if the airline is EU or UK-based (Lufthansa, Air France, British Airways). A US airline flying you into Europe from the US isn't covered this way.


So for Jake, his outbound Chicago–Rome flight on a US airline wasn't covered by EU 261 — that leg falls under DOT rules only. But his return flight, Rome to Chicago, was covered, on the very same US airline, simply because it departed an EU airport. If he'd been bumped on the way home, he'd have been owed up to €600 (roughly $650, though it's paid in euros, not converted at a fixed rate) under EC 261 — separate from, and generally more generous than, the DOT minimum.


The same logic applies specifically to denied boarding: if you're bumped on a flight leaving the EU or UK, you're covered by EC 261/UK 261 no matter who you booked with. If you're bumped on a flight into the EU on a non-EU airline, you're not — you'd fall back on DOT rules instead, which is why what happened to Jake in Denver still matters even on an international itinerary.


One thing you can't do: double-dip. If a flight could technically qualify under both DOT and EU261, you claim under one regime — whichever pays more — not both.[Our EC 261 explainer](https://www.airhelp.com/en/ec-regulation-261-2004/) breaks down the full rule if you want the detail; the AirHelp app checks eligibility under whichever regime applies automatically, so you don't have to work out which rulebook covers your flight yourself.


## How to claim


The legal detail on how oversales work, what counts as a valid fare basis, and how to push back if an airline lowballs the calculation is covered in full on[our overbooking compensation page](https://www.airhelp.com/en/overbooking-compensation/) and our[US passenger rights guide](https://www.airhelp.com/en/flight-rights-usa/) . For the official rulebook, the[DOT's Fly Rights page](https://www.transportation.gov/airconsumer/fly-rights) lays out the full oversales regulation. Or skip the reading: describe what happened in plain language in the AirHelp app, and it checks your eligibility and estimated payout in under a minute.


## Frequently asked questions


#### Do I get compensation if the airline reroutes me and I only lose an hour?


No. If the substitute flight is scheduled to arrive within one hour of your original time, no compensation is required.


#### What if I volunteer to give up my seat?


There's no legal minimum — whatever you negotiate with the airline at the gate is the deal, often a voucher. It's worth asking what else is on the table before you agree.


#### Does this apply to flight delays and cancellations too?


No — this is one of the few disruptions where US law requires cash compensation. Delays and cancellations don't carry the same guarantee; you're generally limited to a refund or a rebooking.


#### Can I get cash instead of a voucher?


Yes. Airlines must pay involuntary denied boarding compensation by cash or check on the spot; a voucher is only offered as an alternative you're free to decline.
